items.title: [reddit.com] Alcohol prompts brain immune cells to damage support matrix in mice
items.content_html: A study published in *Immunity* found that alcohol exposure prompted microglia, the brain’s immune cells, to break down the extracellular matrix that supports brain cells in mice, contributing to synapse loss and impaired function [sciencealert.com#1][index.hr#1]. The work points to an immune-cell pathway alongside alcohol’s direct effects on neurons. Researchers also examined brain tissue from six deceased people with alcohol use disorder and found signs of matrix disruption compared with controls, but the main experiments involved mice [sciencealert.com#1][index.hr#1]. Neuroscientist Dimitrios Davalos of the Cleveland Clinic, the study’s senior author, said his lab is investigating ways to target microglia or protect the matrix. The findings do not establish that an intervention would prevent brain damage in people.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Dementia cases are expected to more than double by 2050. A new study reveals who’s most at risk
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

More and more of our loved ones could develop dementia, as the number of diagnoses is projected to more than double by 2050, according to new research.

In the absence of large-scale prevention efforts, the number of people who are diagnosed with dementia each year could total 24.7 million by 2050, up from 11.4 million in 2023, according to a study by Australian researchers published in JAMA Neurology. Women and people who live in low- and middle-income countries already have higher rates of dementia, a trend that’s likely to continue, according to the findings.

While the researchers didn’t pinpoint an exact reason why dementia affects populations differently, they say the prospect of more cases warrants urgency in investing in prevention efforts. The prospect of 24 million new cases of dementia each year would place “enormous pressure on individuals, families, health systems and economies around the world,” Henry Brodaty, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales Sydney and a co-author of the study, said in a statement.

“We cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond,” Brodaty said. “We need to act across the spectrum—from reducing modifiable risk factors and identifying people at risk earlier, through to improving diagnosis, treatment and care.”

The researchers studied data from more than 38,000 people diagnosed with dementia spanning 18 countries or territories on six continents. They found that the incidence was somewhat higher among women—at 10.6 cases per 1,000 people versus 8.6 for men—but the difference was even starker depending on where people lived. The incidence of dementia was 13.6 cases per 1,000 people in low- and middle-income countries, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.

Understanding the populations who are most at-risk for developing dementia will be key to developing prevention, diagnosis and care strategies, according to the study’s authors. 

“The higher incidence we observed in low- and middle-income countries is particularly concerning because these regions are experiencing rapid population aging while often having the fewest resources for prevention, diagnosis and care,” Perminder Sachdev, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales in Sydney and a senior author of the study, said.

THE FINANCIAL TOLL OF DEMENTIA

Aging populations are understandably one of the main reasons why dementia cases are expected to increase, as this condition that affects memory, thinking and the ability to perform daily activities is more common after the age of 65. As of 2021, an estimated 57 million people worldwide were living with dementia, according to figures from the World Health Organization, and it’s the seventh leading cause of death.

The World Health Organization likewise estimated that as of 2019, dementia cost economies around the world about $1.3 trillion, so a surge in new cases also carries a financial toll. 

That’s why the new research should sound an alarm, as Dr. Liron Sinvani, director of research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging and a professor at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research in New York, told U.S. News & World Report. “It’s an accelerating epidemic that demands immediate attention.” 

And that’s especially important as the countries that will face an “enormous wave” of dementia cases also have very limited infrastructure to respond, as Sinvani told the outlet. 

“Health systems must prepare for this massive increase in diagnostic and care demand, and this is especially true for these low- and middle-income countries where the growth will be fastest,” she said. “We know that dementia care requires a lot of caregiver support and is very costly. We will need a better infrastructure.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
items.content_html:
🌾 🪶 ✏️

As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Strokes have nearly doubled among younger adults, and scientists aren't sure why
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades. Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

items.title: [New Atlas] Decade-long gym steroids study shows just what happens to men's hearts
items.content_html:
One of the first long-term studies that followed weight-training middle-aged men for nearly a decade has found that consistent use of anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS) leads to the thickening of the heart’s left ventricular wall, which increasingly reduces the organ's ability to function. However, this damage was reversed over time after people quit the drugs.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
